extracted.intended_audience: artists, students, and general readers interested in art history and avant-garde practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical techniques for producing Dadaist artworks, performances, and poems — covering aims, media, and specific methods (e.g., cut-up, collage, readymades, sound poetry, photomontage, assemblage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dada aims / anti‑art intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Dada protested the horrors of World War I by rejecting tradition and embracing absurdism, satire, and radical ideas. The manifesto explains that Dada is at its core contradictory and rejects the traditions of art; the related label 'anti‑art' denotes practices that challenge accepted definitions of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants framed their activity as a protest against war, nationalism, and cultural conformity, adopting strategies of nonsense, chance, and ridicule to negate prevailing aesthetic values. Authentic Dada work should manifest rejection of prevailing order, shock common sense, and undermine bourgeois taste and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques and media (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dadaists worked across media, including sound poetry, collage and photomontage (especially in Berlin), and the use of found objects and assemblage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work may span performance, literature, visual collage, three‑dimensional assemblage, and typographic/print experiments. Flexibility across media and cross-disciplinary blending are characteristic and encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-up technique / Tzara's 'TO MAKE A DADAIST POEM'
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed procedural recipe from Tristan Tzara's manifesto: Take a newspaper; take some scissors; choose an article of the desired length; cut out the article; cut out each of the words and put them in a bag; shake gently; take out each cutting in order and copy them — the poem will resemble you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit Dada compositional method emphasizing chance and removal of authorial control; follow the steps literally to produce text reflecting randomness and 'infinitely original' sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chance collage
rubrics_metrics.description: A variation of collage involving dropping torn scraps of paper onto a larger sheet and then pasting the pieces wherever they landed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique foregrounds accident and relinquishes compositional control; use arbitrary placement as a deliberate aesthetic and political gesture against artisanal composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photomontage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of actual or reproductions of real photographs printed in the press, assembled with scissors and glue to express views of modern life; Berlin photomontage often used First World War images for political messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photomontages may emphasize rhetorical (non)relationships among disparate elements rather than realistic continuity; choose press images and juxtapose them to create provocative, political statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblage (three‑dimensional collage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblages are three‑dimensional variations of collage — the assembly of everyday objects (including war objects and trash) to produce meaningful or meaningless pieces of work; objects are nailed, screwed or fastened together and can be seen in the round or hung on a wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use found materials and ordinary detritus; construction methods (nailing, screwing, fastening) and the rawness of materials are part of the aesthetic and message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readymades and readymade variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Marcel Duchamp's practice of designating manufactured objects as art (readymades); sometimes adding signatures, titles, or short sentences — creating 'readymade aided' or 'rectified readymades'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting everyday manufactured objects and recontextualizing them as art (e.g., Fountain) is central. Adding a short sentence or title that 'carries the mind of the spectator towards other regions more verbal' is an established tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Invented by Hugo Ball and pursued by Kurt Schwitters and others: poems that foreground sound over semantic meaning, using nonsense, vocalization, and phonetic play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances may dispense with conventional language; focus on pure sound, rhythm, and the vocal qualities of syllables to subvert journalistic/semantic language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous poems (poèmes simultanés)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems recited by a group of speakers who collectively produce a chaotic and confusing set of voices (simultaneity as an aesthetic device).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple voices speaking at once to create a sonic collage that reflects modern urban noise and advertising; coordination is less important than overlapping chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance tactics: shock, provocation, and vaudevillian excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Dada performances used shock, scandal, provocation, and 'vaudevillian excess' to subvert conventions and protest against war and bourgeois culture; provocations were deliberate and central to the movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately provoke audiences, courts, or critics; use spectacle, scatological or obscene elements, effigies, public demonstrations, incendiary slogans, and theatrical excess to generate scandal and critique institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publications and typographic experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dada circulated through journals and small‑press publications, posters, cards, and broadsides that combined texts, images, and typographic experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use layout, typography, and small‑press formats as part of the work; fragmented type, irregular composition, and experimental printing are authentic Dada strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collage using found ephemera
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending cubist pasting techniques to include items such as transportation tickets, maps, plastic wrappers, and other ephemera to portray aspects of life rather than still life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source materials from quotidian life and mass media; inclusion of ephemera grounds work in the modern urban environment and critiques commodity culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Berlin Dada emphases / political criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups in Germany emphasized political and social activity (corrosive manifestos and propaganda, satire, public demonstrations) and technical discoveries in painting and literature; distinguishing characteristics included 'its political element and its technical discoveries', 'inexhaustible energy', and 'mental freedom which included the abolition of everything'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berlin Dada authenticity leans toward overt political engagement, photomontage as propaganda, public demonstrations, and explicit attacks on institutions and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: New York Dada character (irony and humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: New York Dada tended to be more theoretically driven, less political, and was driven by a sense of irony and humor; New Yorkers called activities 'Dada' but did not issue manifestos, preferring challenges via exhibitions and publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize irony, wit, and conceptual provocation (e.g., readymades, gallery challenges) rather than overt political agitation; publication‑based critique and institutional challenge are valid forms.
